utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. May I remind you, sir, the affirmation you made still applies. Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Keskovski.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, you testified I believe the day before yesterday that on August -- on 11 August, you were in the president's cabinet that morning. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And it was a quiet day, so you decided to go home and have lunch at around 2.30, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: You indicated that at around 3.00 you received a phone call from the president, and he asked you where you were, you explained to him that you were having lunch, and he said he wanted to join you, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: He was at your home between 3.00 and 5.00 that day. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And while you were having your lunch, you received a telephone call from the prime minister's cabinet, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: You were informed that there were skirmishes in Radusa and the prime minister asked for assistance from the army, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So what happened was the prime minister needed to contact the president for assistance, because the prime minister could only issue orders to the police and only the president could issue orders to the army, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called from the cabinet of the prime minister to ask for assistance from the army. This is what I know. Why, I don't know. I presume this is because the president can issue orders to the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: You received information?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Simply before my colleague goes any further I would like to correct the record; she has put a proposition to the witness in relation to the evidence which he gave two days ago, and I believe it was at page 1004 going on 1005, the witness both in his evidence-in-chief and in his OTP statement mentioned that the president arrived, at around 5.00 at his home, not as 3.00 as indicated by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm just going to carry on, Your Honour. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, sir, you received information about the position of the soldiers on the ground from the prime minister's office, and you passed this information on to the president, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I should say you received information about the position of the police on the ground. Is that right? Or the security forces.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, about the security forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And the prime minister, of course, could get information from the Ministry of Interior, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can guess yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And I'd like just to go to P464, which is tab 3 in the Prosecution binder. And for the e-court purposes, it would be N006-3017 to N006-3033 at page 8 in the English version; and in the Macedonian, it's pages 106 to 107. Now, I draw your attention, Mr. Keskovski, to the -- this is actually a segment from a book called, titled, the war in Macedonia in 2001, and I draw your attention to the passage underneath the heading, orders, the use of the police during -- should say state of war to support the army. And it say: "Since a state of war was not declared," than is starting about the third paragraph underneath that passage, "the police was not under Joint Command and acted independently. One can only imagine what the situation is like when two ministers from the same government, the Ministry of Interior, and the Ministry of Defence, have two armed components at their disposal, one of which is commanded by the prime minister through the minister of the interior, while the other is under the command of the president of the Republic through the defence minister." "The two ministers from differing political provinces rather than enduring on the course of joint defence of the national and state interests in such a complicated and dangerous situation seem to be fighting for elevated positions in their parties, the government and the Defence. As a result, it could be said that the two armed structures, the police and the army, were each fighting on their own front." You see that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And no state of war had been declared in 2001, had it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, getting back to the telephone call that came from the prime minister's cabinet, before that telephone call, the president didn't mention anything to you about any skirmishes or battles going on in the region that he was particularly concerned about while you were having lunch with him, did he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the area of Radusa?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Or any other area -- or any other battles in the region, did he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In continuity the public was informing about sporadic skirmishes of the security forces in the region of Ljuboten and in the region Radusa. On the 10th and on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well in the transcript, what you say here is: In continuity the public was informing sporadic skirmishes. Are you talking about the media, Mr. Keskovski?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the media, and public reports from the institutions. This was public information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. But at that point, the president didn't discuss this -- didn't discuss any concerns he had with you or anything about any -- any plans for an operation going on during the course of your lunch, did he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, on August -- the 12th of August, 2001, you then went to the cabinet of the president at around 9.00 to 10.00 in the morning, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And this was a very important day for the president and his cabinet because the signing of the Ohrid Framework Agreement was scheduled for the next day, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was an important day, but the cabinet was not in full composition because we had the cabinet had completed all the preliminary preparations. It was an important day because we were receiving the delegations, their advance teams and there was plenty of work for the security.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. But there was so much work to do within the cabinet for the -- for -- in preparation for the international delegations that the president did not even go to church that Sunday, did he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And the signing of the Ohrid Agreement was the most important issue that day for all members of the president's office, including the president, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, the signing was the next day. You didn't understand me that the signing was on the 13th. But this was an important day, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but I'm referring to the preparations of that day. And as you say in paragraph 49 of your statement and you can refer to your statement if you wish. It's at tab 1 of the Prosecution binder. Because of the importance of that day, the preparatory work that was being carried out, nobody in the president's office was paying attention to what was going on in Ljuboten, were they?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you testified yesterday, Mr. Keskovski, around -- at 10022 to 10023 in the transcript, that the president called you in -- in his office that day and told you that there were activities in Ljuboten and the area of Ljubanci and he wanted you to contact Ljube Boskoski immediately. You recall testify to go that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: If I can please refer you to paragraph 50 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And for the record it's 65 ter 1D1249.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: What you say in your statement: "The president told me that he had information that something was happening in Radisani village and he could not reach the minister of the interior, Ljube Boskoski. He wanted to talk to him so he tasked me to get in touch with Ljube Boskoski." Isn't that what you said in your statement, Mr. Keskovski?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: To the extent that my colleague is intent on suggesting a contradiction between what was said yesterday and the statement, could we have the correct page of the transcript which she is referring because the statement of yesterday as we have it appears to finish at 1019 and we see no reference on that page to the reference given by our colleague. So if she could refer to that page so it can be verified.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, the transcript from yesterday begins at the very bottom of 10022 over to the top of 10023 which are the pages that I referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now in your statement, Mr. Keskovski, you gave a very specific answer to a very specific question in 2005 when you were asked by the investigators and you told them that the president was concerned about something happening in Radisani, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this. This is correct but not when asked a specific question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, nevertheless, in your statement, you refer to a concern the president had about the village of Radisani, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement of 2005, but also in my statements of my current testimony, I said that the president knew of ongoing activities in the area of the village of Ljubanci and that, as a consequence, there was movement of civilian population in the area of the village of Radisani. This is in the context of what I have said and in this context, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Keskovski, just so that the record is entirely clear, I'm going to read to you what you said yesterday when you were asked this question by Mr. Mettraux. You were asked at the bottom of page 1022 of the transcript a question: "And what did he tell you, if anything at that point? Mr. Mettraux is referring to the president. And your answer is: "The president called me in told me that in Ljuboten and in the area of Ljubanci there have been some activities and that he wants to establish contact immediately with the minister of the interior, Mr. Ljube Boskoski; on his order, I attempted to find the minister. However, I was unable to establish contact with him. This is a telephone number which I had memorised in my mobile phone. And then you're asked another question. And the following question was: "Did the president tell you who he had got than information from about things happening in Ljuboten and Ljubanci? And you answer: "He did not tell me who he received this information from." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the opportunity to see this. I can only hear what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. You have heard out what I read out to you, the questions and the answers that you were asked and the answers that you gave yesterday, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I repeated the same today. I believe I have said the same thing today.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, just so we're clear about this, Mr. Keskovski, what do you mean when you say, I believe that you've said the same thing today?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't say, I believe. Perhaps this is how it was interpreted to you. The same thing which you read out to me now, I also said two minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: But that's not what you said in your statement 2005, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you read the statement which I gave in 2005 as a whole, you will come to the same information. If you like, I will repeat it again. The president --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- If you like I can repeat it again, the same statement which I gave then and which I'm giving now in the same context.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: There's no need for you to repeat it again, Mr. Keskovski. Now, you said, you testified, that the president was concerned about the activities in the region in your statement you said Radisani village; now you're saying Ljuboten. And he summonsed you because on this critical morning, the president could not reach the minister of the interior, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you divide two things of the same event, which encompass the same event, the events regarding Ljubanci. I said this in my statement of 2005, that something was happening with the civilian population who had gathered in the area of the village of Radisani. I think this is what I told you yesterday and in 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the Prosecutor has to -- if there is a suggestion, which apparently is attempted to be made that Mr. Keskovski has changed what he said and that as the Prosecutor said he would have said at the time that he was concerned about the activities in the region of Radisani and that is he now saying that he was concerned about Ljuboten, at paragraph 51 of the witness statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness has just referred to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He's made it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But in his statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Don't worry. We fully realise 51 is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And I was just getting to that, actually, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now Mr. Keskovski, when the president summonsed you on this critical morning, it was because he could not reach the minister of the interior, Ljube Boskoski, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not because he was unable to get in touch with him. Because this was a Sunday. His cabinet was not working on a regular base. That is to say, his secretaries were not on duty that day, so he called me since I was able to establish contact with all the institutions which he needed to contact, be it from the Republic of Macedonia or abroad. The people who were on duty on Saturday or Sunday -- and Sunday did not have the information how to get in touch. Therefore, these were extraordinary activities so he called me in. This was the usual practice of how things were done, not on only on the 12th. This was the regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. But the president was so concerned about getting in touch with Ljube Boskoski that he essentially forced you to cancel a meeting that had you planned with your subordinates that day because he wanted you to try to reach the minister, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not right. I've never said that I've cancelled the meeting. Prior to starting the meeting, the president called me in, and I think this is what I said then and what I'm saying now, today. I did not cancel the meeting, because this was a very important meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. You postponed the meeting in order to get in touch with Ljube Boskoski. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to the starting of the meeting, I did not start it because it had not begun yet. The meeting with the security group of the president. You can interpret it in a way you would like, but this has been my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: The reason that the president needed you to speak to Minister Boskoski is because he was concerned that the escalation of events and violence in Radisani and Ljubanci might have a negative effect on the signing of the Ohrid Agreement, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president was concerned; this is correct. He did not ask of me to speak with Mr. Boskoski but to establish contact with him so as he be able to speak with Mr. Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: You tried to reach Minister Boskoski on his phones but you couldn't reach him, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So the president instructed you to contact the prime minister's cabinet, to see if they can reach the minister, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me to call the cabinet of the prime minister so that they can give me guidelines how we can establish contact with the minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And someone from the prime minister's cabinet gave you the number for Ljube Boskoski's driver, and that's how you reached Minister Boskoski, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated, this was Mr. Robert Ljusev from the cabinet of the prime minister, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So the prime minister's cabinet knew how to get in touch with Minister Boskoski, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They gave me telephone numbers where I can -- which I can turn and try to and get in touch with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And that's because the prime minister and Minister Boskoski were actually quite close, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: When you reached Minister Boskoski, the president spoke to the minister and asked him about the situation in Radisani and if he knew anything else that was happening there, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: The president ordered, as you said, at 10025, page 10025 in the transcript, that the president ordered Mr. Boskoski to go to Radisani and with his authority to calm down the crowds and forbid them from going into the village of Ljubanci, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So Minister Boskoski had the authority to calm the situation down, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the president believed in this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And going back to paragraph 51 of your statement, Mr. Keskovski, you mention there that the population was angry and you do refer to the villages of Radisani and Ljubanci, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: You don't, however, refer to the village of Ljuboten, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you read well the paragraph, it reads [In English] In the village of Radisani and Ljubanci, [Interpretation] In Ljuboten there is no Macedonian population. You have not read the paragraph fully, so, yes, this is correct. In the region of Radisani and Ljubanci, if you say -- you Ljubanci means Ljubanci and Radisani or if you mention Radisani this is also Ljuboten and Ljubanci because these are all villages within a parameter of two kilometres. If you look at the map, this will become clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And so if the president was so concerned, Mr. Keskovski, that interethnic clashes might negatively impact on the signing of the framework agreement would you expect the president to add fuel to those interethnic clashes by ordering an operation in the village of Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position of the president and of the entire state leadership during that period was in order to sign the framework agreement and because of the pressure of the Macedonian population during that period, the positions of the army of the Republic of Macedonia and of the security forces to be restored back behind the line of 5th of July, 2001, which was endangered by the Albanian terrorist groups, otherwise, there would have been great unrest and the signing of the framework agreement would not be facilitated. I believe that I was not the only one who said that. You read it yourself as well, several times.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the counsel to speak closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The operations that you now mention are part of the pushing the structures of the Albanian terrorist groups back behind the lines of 5th of July that the NATO guaranteed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, you mention, Mr. Keskovski, in paragraph 53 of your statement after the president spoke to Ljube Boskoski and told him to calm the situation down that you received a request from the president to make a inquiry if you had someone that you knew in Ljuboten, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And asked me specifically about Mr. Tarculovski, to make contact with him, I think this is also written in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. But right now we're dealing with the part of your statement where you said that the president requested from -- for you to make an inquiry if you had someone that you knew in Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then continues in my statement and asked me specifically to establish contact with Mr. Tarculovski, because what you are asking me is now outside of the context of the sentence. You can't ask the question in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I didn't ask you another -- a question yet, Mr. Keskovski. I simply asked you if you -- I simply referring you to your statement or that portion of your statement. If the president, Mr. Keskovski, was in control of an operation, would he inquire if you knew someone in Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to say that at no moment I stated that the president had the control over the operation, and you are trying to lead me to something completely different, which I had not stated. This means that this is your conclusion. I haven't stated this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. So you're now telling us that the president did not have control over the operation in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying either of the two. It is you who are saying it. It is you making the statement. I haven't said anything. You made the conclusion and you're asking me whether the conclusion was correct. I told you that such phrasing or such words I have not used in none of my statements that I gave. If you are interpreting it that way, then this is your conclusion. I haven't made any such conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right. So I'll ask you more directly then. As far as you you're telling us, did the president have control over the operation in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I answer this?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Are you saying you don't know?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've also said, as you just mentioned moments ago, or you repeated moments ago, that the president asked you about Johan Tarculovski whose phone was off the whole time. That's what you say in paragraph 53 of your statement. Well, Mr. Keskovski, if Johan Tarculovski was supposed to be reporting on the operation in Ljuboten to the president, why would Johan make himself unavailable to the president?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why are you asking this question of me?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm asking you the question. It's my job. My job is to ask you questions and your job is to answer them.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only conjecture on this question. I can't answer precisely, accurately, since I am not involved in the question that you are asking. Why Johan Tarculovski was unavailable if the president wished -- why was Johan Tarculovski -- the president wanted to have contact with him. Where I am involved in this? Where is my specific knowledge about this question that you are asking me? I don't know. My answer is I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. And on that day, as you say in paragraph 53 of your statement, you weren't aware of anything else happening in regards to Ljuboten, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And after 13 August, after the Ohrid Agreement had been signed on that day, Johan Tarculovski, you testified, returned to work a few days later, and you later heard, you've told us, that -- from the media that Johan Tarculovski was involved in the operation in Ljuboten. That's what you've told us in your testimony, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot later. This is what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically some ten months later.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. So ten months later, that was the first time that you heard that Johan Tarculovski was involved in the Ljuboten operation, through media reports. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you said that you asked him about his involvement or his -- what was reported in the media about his involvement in the Ljuboten operation, and he denied it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Didn't the president also ask Johan Tarculovski about his involvement in the Ljuboten operation, Mr. Keskovski?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened at the same time and at the same place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, just to be -- so that we're absolutely clear about what you're telling us, I'd like you to please turn to paragraph 57 of your statement, please. Do you have it there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, you say in paragraph 57: "Being asked if I asked Johan Tarculovski to comment on the writings on certain newspapers that he was heavily involved in Ljuboten events, he answered briefly that it was rubbish and that he was in Ljubanci all the time." And then you say: "The president asked him also the same question in my presence and Tarculovski gave him the same answer." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And I stated this also now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So the president specifically asked about Johan -- asked Johan Tarculovski whether he was involved in the Ljuboten operation, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, at that happened at the same time, the same place that. Was not a separate meeting that was not a separate occasion and it was not formal. This happened informally while we were walking. We met Johan Tarculovski, we asked him. It was written in the media today that you were involved. Were you involved? And the answer was that these were speculations. That's all. That's all that happened. Everything that I asked and what I saw the president asking. I don't know about any other thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move to a different topic. Now, in 2001, Mr. Keskovski, you instructed your subordinates in your sector to contact you before trying to get in touch with any other members of the Ministry of Interior, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is not an order issued in 2000. The order is from the beginning of the functioning of the group for security of the president.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a general order. It dates a lot earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. So you had a general order to your -- that you had given to your subordinates, perhaps even prior to 2001, that they must contact you before trying to get in touch with any other members of the Ministry of Interior, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with other members of the Ministry of Interior. I have given a precise statement. I really elaborated what I meant by this precisely. All needs, individual needs of members of the sector for internal affairs, and members of our group from the Ministries of the Interior and the Ministry of Defence regarding all their personal private needs, they need to speak first to our sector and through our sector address the Ministry of Interior. There is due to security reasons, since it could happen that there would be leakage of information to two ministries that are of different nature, information from the cabinet of the president might leak there. We have had such case in the year 2000 and this is why we have made such decision in coordination with the president.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, if can I refer you to paragraph 30 of your statement, Mr. Keskovski, you say, the second sentence of paragraph 30: "My personnel had the orders to contact me before trying to get in touch with any other officers in the Ministry of Interior including the minister of the interior personally. All the requests were coming through me. I was the only person responsible and the one who could give answers to the minister of the interior regarding the president's security matters." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, and I believe that it is very specific. What I said now is identical to what you have read out now. It is exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So regarding security matters, the -- your members had to get in touch with you before contacting other members of the Ministry of Interior, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But I will tell you again. With regards to their personal needs, if it concerns the regular activities of the sector, then they had regular contacts with other services that would be involved in any operation of ours. That is standard. They couldn't call me to ask that the advance team contacts the traffic police. This is something trivial.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So when you say with regards to their personal needs, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personal needs that every employee of any institution might have. There are various issues that the ministry covers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Can you provide an example?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If someone has been employed as a person with secondary education and then wishes to have acknowledged the higher education that they have acquired in the meantime, they need to address the ministry. But in order to address the ministry to have this on record, they need to address us first and we, through official channels address the ministry. This is one of the examples.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. So if I understand what you're saying then, you're saying that in regards to --

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will give you another example, a different one. If they wish to be issued with any equipment, they first needed to inform us that they want to go to be issued with equipment, and then they go to the Ministry of Interior to be issued with equipment. This is yet another example. I'm speaking about personal equipment. Maybe a communication station has broken down or something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So in regards to perhaps employment matters or human resources matters or getting -- issuing personal equipment, they needed to go through you. That's what you're telling us, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And that's because you wanted to ensure that the chain of command was respected. Right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I stated already, we have had cases in the year 2000 when information leaked from the president's office, from this reason --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Keskovski, I heard your answer before. I'm now asking you a different question, and I'd just like you to answer this question, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me now the question that I have ordered this because I wanted the chain of command to function. I told you, why was it that I have made this order? Before this order was made in 2000 the contacts between the members of the sector for security of the president and any other sector, they could have communicated directly with all institutions within the ministry. And I explained why I made that order and why that procedure needed to be followed, and this does not apply only to the Ministry of Interior but the same applied also to the Ministry of Defence. I believe I clarified this already.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when members of your unit or sector were not on duty, they would not necessarily inform you of every activity that they carried out while they were on leave, would they?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is not within the remit of the service, yes. With regards to their private activities, they don't have any need to inform me, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So you wouldn't be aware of who they were communicating with, for example, with regards to activities outside the remit of the service?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So if a member of your unit, for example, communicated with a member of the prime minister's security, you may not be aware of that, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'd like to please go to P369, and that's at tab 12 of the binder. And perhaps it might be easier to display the Macedonian version on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now for Madam Registrar, I will be first referring to e-court page 22, N000-7433, 022 in the English and Macedonian. Now, Mr. Keskovski, this is a telephone log-book, which is believed to belong to Johan Tarculovski. And if I can -- these are records of the phone calls that are pertaining to Johan Tarculovski. And if I can ask you to turn to page 22 in your hard copy, or simply look on your screen. Should be 21 in your hard copy. And if you can look at about the third line from the bottom of that page. Now, this record indicates that Johan Tarculovski made a telephone call to Vlatko Stefanovski on the 19th of August, 2001. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: If we can please go to page 58 in e-court, both in the Macedonian and English version. And page 3 of the outgoing -- or incoming calls, rather, in the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, at about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, Your Honour, but the Defence would simply ask Ms. Issa to identify, if she is able to the basis upon which the Prosecution is able to determine that the phone call was in fact made to Mr. Stefanovski, and if the sole basis for that assertion is in fact the document that the Prosecutor has put in front of the witness. We are aware of a number of matters that perhaps not want to state those in front of the witness, but if she could identify this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would think it not appropriate to interrupt the cross-examination for that purpose, Mr. Mettraux. She's proceeding on the basis of this exhibit which has been tendered and used on that basis to date. Please continue, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Mr. Keskovski, if you can please look to about the 11th line from the top on that page on the screen, and you'll see at about that portion of the page, this is a record indicating that there was a telephone call made to the number pertaining to Johan Tarculovski from someone in the security of the prime minister on the 11th of August, 2001. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And if I can just ask for the following page to be displayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask my learned colleague when asking the question to use the term "telephone number which we believe was used by Mr. Johan Tarculovski." Since she did this on previously on page 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will do, Mr. Apostolski. Yes, I think the cross-examination can proceed. Both yourself and Mr. Mettraux are anxious to make points that can be made at other times very effectively but not in the course of cross-examination. Thank you. Carry on, please, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, on the following page, Mr. Keskovski, at about the 11th line from the top, once again, we see an incoming call. The record indicates there is an incoming call from the security of the prime minister to the number -- to Johan Tarculovski. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Were you aware, Mr. Keskovski, that Johan Tarculovski was in contact with Vlatko Stefanovski and the prime minister's security on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: If I can then please ask for page 44 in e-court to be displayed?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, at around the middle of that page, Mr. Keskovski, this record indicates that there was a telephone call from Johan Tarculovski to Goran Stojkov on the 4th of August, 2001. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot see it. The screen is split in two, and I can only see the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: If I might just ask that we show the Macedonian version, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And, finally, Mr. Keskovski -- If I can ask Madam Registrar to please go to page 47 in e-court, in the Macedonian version. And it's page 46 in the hard copy English version. Now, at the bottom of that page, Mr. Keskovski, there are several calls, and the record indicates that those calls were made from Johan Tarculovski's phone to Goran Stojkov on the 6th of August, 2001. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I should be looking at a different page. But now I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware that Johan Tarculovski made or had contact with Goran Stojkov during that period, Mr. Keskovski?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And during that time, in August 2001, Goran Stojkov was working at the prime minister's security section, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, you've explained, Mr. Keskovski, that Johan Tarculovski's duty was to follow and secure the movement of the first lady, right, in your sector?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these were the duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And he was reporting everything regarding the first lady's security matters directly to you or to your deputies, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He informed Mr. Jarcev, myself or the deputies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And in the branch that he used to work in, the hours of his work were more flexible because the level of security for the first lady was much lower than that of the president, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And the making of the schedule was left up to that branch. You were not involved in the scheduling of his duties or in that branch, were you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a regular basis, no. In certain circumstances when this was requested by the president, yes. But in regular activities, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And because the schedule was more flexible in that branch, sometimes Johan Tarculovski and others working out of that branch worked two or three days and then had two or three days rest, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: You were asked yesterday at page 10034 of the transcript whether it was correct that Johan Tarculovski was in charge of the security for the first lady also during her official and private trips, that was the question that you asked [sic] And you answered yes. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you to paragraph 19 of your statement, Mr. Keskovski, please. Now, that says, what you've said to the investigators in your statement: "Regarding Johan Tarculovski's duties as the first lady's security, I would like to say that in the branch he used to work the making of the schedule was left to them, since the level of security was much lower than that of the president. Sometimes they would work two or three days and then have two or three days rest. It was very flexible. Johan Tarculovski's duty was following and securing any movement of the first lady. Johan Tarculovski has never been the direct security inspector of the then president." Now I'd like you to go to paragraph 23. And you say there: "I do not remember where the first lady was during that time." And in the previous paragraph the last sentence refers to August or the month of August. "I just remember that sometime in under/July and the beginning of August 2001, she was in London and then she came back for a short period of time and travelled to Turkey. But I do not remember the exact itinerary, but it is easy to verify her movement within the Ministry of Interior or more specifically at police station in charge of border crossing points in Macedonian. And then you say: "Johan Tarculovski was not with the first lady when she was abroad. I recall that I saw Johan Tarculovski in Ohrid but I do not remember the exact days when he was there. I gave them more rest time since the lady was not in the country that they could relax a bit. But when Johan Tarculovski was in Ohrid with the team, he didn't receive any special order from me." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So just to clarify, then, Mr. Keskovski, Johan Tarculovski was not with the first lady during that period of time when she was abroad, was he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is what I think in that period during those travels, since they were of a special nature, none of the security of the first lady did not go with her. In Great Britain for sure, because this is a trip organised by MI-6 to provide security of the first lady.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody knew whether she was in Macedonia or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like it go to another topic now. Now, you testified at various points, Mr. Keskovski, that you would go off to Vaksince, or you have been to Vaksince, Tetovo and other places, and you gathered information or intelligence for the president, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that on the order of the president, I went to -- I was in several places from Tetovo the Lipkovo region, Lipkovo-Kumanovo region, Aracinovo, and other places with an order to report from the ground and this meant that I communicate, if I may say, officers from the army and from the police, and to inform about the course of the activities on given orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say to gather intelligence information, because this could not have happened. This was a crisis situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. But you're telling us that you were sent by the president specifically to gather information for him and to report back to him, in relation to all of these -- as to what was happening in all of these areas that you've just listed, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, there was, at the time in 2001, Mr. Keskovski, there was an intelligence branch or service for the government who gather information and intelligence regarding matters that are relevant to the given time, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And the army has its own intelligence branch. It's called G-2, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sector for security, or, rather, sector for intelligence in the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And the minister of the interior has its own intelligence service, the DBK, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think when you previously asked me, you were asking about intelligence service. This is a service under the authority of the president, while the next question you're asking me is probably about the DBK, which is within the MOI. This is not for intelligence; rather, for counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. So all of these agencies whose job was to gather information regarding, in part, at the time, the crisis, were out there, and you're saying that the president would task you and people from your sector, like Johan Tarculovski, to gather information for him, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of what you're wanting to ask me, I will answer specifically. All these services which you listed collect information and once a day, or once a week, inform the institutions about the situation on the ground. The president issued me with a task about a concrete operation which I was supposed to inform him about, from the ground. I will repeat, I did not collect intelligence and such information about operations. Again, I'm speaking about operations reporting from operations. I'm not speaking about collecting intelligence on the ground. This is a lengthy activity. I told you, I was sent on the ground to inform him about the operations and the activities specifically for the Aracinovo case. He send me at the onset of the action, on the positions of the army and police in Brnjanci from there I established contact with him. I gave him the commander of the special unit of the police to inform him directly how the situation stands on the ground. These were my tasks. When I returned, I gave him a report that the action in Aracinovo will not be successful as early as Friday, and so forth and so on. I think I'm being very specific in my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Keskovski, doesn't the army report about operations that are ongoing on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president had information that some things which were happening on the ground were not represented to him in a proper fashion and I said this. This was the reason why Pande Petrovski was removed and replaced as chief of General Staff. I think I stated this precisely yesterday. This is why there was a need for a direct contact, and when I say "direct," I mean not with intermediaries but direct. His eyes on the ground. Mr. Keskovski, wasn't there -- doesn't the Ministry of Interior report about operations on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you do not understand me or do not want to understand me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Mr. Keskovski --

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I'm speak being now. If an operation is ongoing now, I have to report now not to write a report about the work or this operation. These are two different things at hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And if the president wanted a report, a specific report about an operation, couldn't he have, for example called the chief of General Staff and perhaps gotten a report from him about some operation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He surely has done this, but he believed he wanted to hear something directly from people with -- in whom he has maximum trust. As I said previously, his eyes and his ears on the ground. Why did he send me to Aracinovo? In the activity in Aracinovo, so that he can establish contact with the commanders and not only with those leading the operation but also from the other commanders who were on the ground of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Couldn't the -- couldn't the president have contacted Minister Ljube Boskoski to get information from him on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Surely he had called Minister Boskoski and the chief of General Staff and the minister of defence. However he also sent me on the ground, where I was almost shot. I spent four hours in ambush in Aracinovo. He would not have sent me in these clashes to die if there was no need to that end. It was not my work duty. It was an order of the president.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So the president didn't really trust Ljube Boskoski to get him the direct information, did he? That's why he needed to send you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot respond and answer this question. How can I tell you whether the president trusted Mr. Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, you've just told us that the president sent you instead of obtaining his informs from all these other possible organisations, because he needed somebody there that he could trust. Right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly right, and I said he wanted to get in touch or establish contact with commanders who were commanding directly on the ground, not only with the leadership and the leading command. I'm sure he had contacts with all of those, with the MOI and the minister, the Ministry of Defence and the minister and the chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Didn't he trust Minister Boskoski, for example, to give him the complete and accurate information as to what was going on, on the ground.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He trusted Minister Boskoski because, as I previously said, he had sent him on previous other places. He also placed Minister Buckovski because he was in daily contact with him and gave him information. I presume he also trusted Mr. Pande Petrovski, because they were in daily contact but all these three together are in no correlation with the tasks which I received. I think I explained this clearly. Direct information does not mean commanders on the ground through the heads of the services where they are assigned to, to the president. He wanted to be in direct contact to see if they were encountering problems during the action and not with the police only but the army as well. When-- if you were to ask me if President Trajkovski trusted Mr. Boskoski, then you will have to ask me whether he also trusted Mr. Buckovski, the chief of General Staff and all the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that obviously my colleague did not do that on purpose but that to the extent that she wishes to put to the witness a proposition that she should suggest he has made, she should do that fairly and correctly; and in the question when there was a suggestion that the president sent you, that would be Mr. Keskovski, instead of obtaining his information from other source this is a serious distortion of what he said. It there was no suggestion that it was an either or situation. It was repeatedly stated that it was and, that both information had come from certain places and that in addition he sent Mr. Keskovski. I think it has to be fair to the witness and not seek to distort the evidence that has been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. May I make it clear once again that where a witness is likely to be misled by a question, you can expect the Chamber to interfere. When a question is put that the witness is very capable of dealing with, as you have just heard, we will not interfere. It's just an unnecessary delaying of the process. But a witness the capacity to deal with things and make his position clear, as this witness is, we will leave that matter alone and let the witness show what he really means, as he is capable of doing and the end result is more satisfactory for non-interference.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this a convenient time now, Ms. Issa?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Before we move on to another topic, Mr. Keskovski, you mentioned in the last session, before the recess, that when the president sent you on the ground, you were almost shot and you spent hours in ambush and that was it was not your work duty. And that was at page 32 of today's transcript, lines 6 to 12. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall the event as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So sometimes, because of the complexity of the security situation in 2001, people such as yourself worked, carried out duties, or carried out tasks that were outside of their normal duties, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I stated. The regular duties were on the one hand, but upon the president's order, those, again, became regular duties, because the president had ordered those.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, I'd like just to move to another topic. You explained in your examination-in-chief that on 11 August 2001 Johan Tarculovski called you from Ljubanci and said that there was an action being planned in Ljuboten, and that this was shortly after 5.00, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And as you say in paragraph 39 of your statement, you asked him what it means, and he replied that in Ljuboten there are fortifications of terrorists. Now, you asked him that question, because at this point, did you not know what Johan was talking about, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Johan told you that the police and army units were involved in preparing the action, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: You asked him what the problem was, and he explained to you that there was a lack of cooperation from an army major who did not want to undertake the action without orders, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And that was the first time that you'd heard of this action, when Johan called you and told you about it.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, apart from the issues with the army major, Johan never mentioned any problems with anyone else, did he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: He never said anything about any problems with the police, did he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And the nature of the problem, with the army major, was that the major did not want to undertake any activities until the major received an order from his army superiors, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So you asked the major what was his rank and who was his immediate superior, and he -- the major told you that his superior was army General Sokol Mitrevski, who was the president's agitant, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: You also asked the army major if the major would obey an order from the president, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And the major replied that he would, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you say in paragraph 40 - and you testified, I believe - in your statement that you were still holding on to the phone and you explained to the president the situation, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And, incidentally, you testified that the president spoke to Johan Tarculovski before he spoke to the army major. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: But if we look in your statement, particularly at paragraph 40, there's nothing in there that says that the president spoke directly to Johan Tarculovski at this point, is there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What they asked me, I answered. I am standing behind my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, when the president spoke to Major Despodov, he asked the major about his rank and who his superior was, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And you heard the president tell the major that he would call Sokol Mitrevski, who was the superior of Major Despodov, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told the major the following: Undertake all actions within your competence so that the operation, the action there, is successful, and I will phone General Sokol Mitrevski.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. So the president wanted to make sure that any orders he issued would be issued down the proper chain of command. That's why he said he would phone Sokol Mitrevski. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president had already issued an order at a lower level, and he said he would inform General Sokol Mitrevski of the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And why was it then necessary for the president to inform Sokol Mitrevski of the order?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since he was the supreme commander of the armed forces of the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So, in other words, the president wanted to make sure that the hierarchy or the higher levels of the chain of command within the army were aware of what was going on, that there was an order issued, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, Major Despodov was a major in the army, and his superiors, as you just mentioned, was Sokol Mitrevski and also General Stamboliski. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you follow the line of hierarchy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, when you spoke to Johan Tarculovski, didn't you ask him why Major Despodov's superiors didn't order Despodov to undertake the action?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was -- I -- there was no need of me to interfere when the president has issued the orders, to Johan, also to go and inform him. On had a basis would I ask Johan all these questions that you are now putting to me? If I had been the one sending Johan to the grounds then maybe I would ask him, but I had no authority to send him to the ground to perform tasks that are outside of the scope of his working tasks set forth in the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: If there was an action organised by the president, which involved the president's army, why wouldn't General Stamboliski have contacted the president instead of Johan Tarculovski contacting the president?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I don't understand your question. Since we have here two different things. You're asking me about the General Stamboliski and about Johan Tarculovski. I can't understand you. Would be kind to ask your question again, or to ask it more precisely?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: If there was an action organised by the president which involved the president's army, why didn't the Chief of Staff, or perhaps Major Despodov's superiors, or General Stamboliski -- members of the army have contacted the president about the major refusing to undertake an action instead of Johan Tarculovski contacting the president?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you need to ask this question of Major Despodov or what was his name? You said it. I don't know his name. Whether he was able to establish contact with his superiors in the highest ranks so then for this communication to continue. I can't answer the question whether and how was the major able to establish contact so that this chain of command would be followed further across the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now that day, there were no other contacts from Johan Tarculovski or anyone else relating to this matter, was there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And as far as you were aware, the president did not contact Sokol Mitrevski, did he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: While he was with me? No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, in 2001, Mr. Keskovski, when an action is being prepared by the security forces, that fact is not generally made known to the public, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And that's because in 2001 the security forces issued confidential orders and plans for operations because if such orders and plans became publicly known they might alert the enemy to the security forces's preparation, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Due to security reasons. This is what should be written.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. So the security forces are very careful about information that may be divulged, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: You've testified that when Johan Tarculovski called you and told you there was a problem with an army major that, as far as you were aware, Johan Tarculovski did not tell you that he, Johan, was involved in the operation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: In fact, as far as you knew, Johan was in Ljubanci, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And after 13 August, when Johan returned to work, some ten months later, and you asked him about news of his involvement in the Ljuboten action, he denied it, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, if Johan Tarculovski was not involved in this operation, how do you explain the fact that Johan Tarculovski knew there was a problem with Major Despodov?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my own experience I can give you an example, if you accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking you to give me an example. I'm asking you how you explain the fact that Johan Tarculovski knew there was a problem within the army chain of command or with the army major, Despodov?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was sent by the president of the state to Aracinovo during the action to seize Aracinovo village in the region of Brnjanci, I was sent to a task similar to the one given to Mr. Tarculovski with regards to Ljubanci region. From what I heard, this is what I gather, that they were similar. When I got there, the general, the commander of the special unit of the police, communicated to us that they had a problem with -- because they didn't have a tank there in the region where they were active. So I phoned the president directly, personally and informed him about the problems that were identified in order to have him directly aware of the problems that the commanders were having in the field. In this context, Mr. Tarculovski could have known about certain problems that had emerged on the ground with regards to coordination between the security forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: But in this case, unlike the case you just described to us, Mr. Keskovski, you explained earlier in your testimony, and as it states at paragraph 34 of your statement, that the president had asked Johan Tarculovski to inform him about the situation in the village and that the president was concerned about unrest in the village. Right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not regarding the unrest in the village. I believe that I hadn't given such statement, if we're speaking about the 10th of August, 2001. I said that Mr. Boris Trajkovski, the president, had ordered Mr. Tarculovski, when going to the village of Ljubanci, because he had a personal issue there, he requested to be -- to go there and then to -- the president requested that he be informed about the situation on the ground by Mr. Tarculovski, since the situation was well known that -- the public was aware of it also. That after the action of the Albanian terrorists and the killing of the eight soldiers, there was still sporadic fighting between the Macedonian security forces and the Albanian terrorists in the area of village of Ljuboten. The concern of the president was that maybe there was the intention for this conflict to escalate to an even higher level because threats were made that the city of Skopje would be shelled and that would have placed the signing of the Ohrid Framework Agreement under risk. I believe I explained it better now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, if you look at paragraph 34 of your statement, Mr. Keskovski, what is say there is that you "heard the president asking Johan Tarculovski to call the next day and inform the president about the situation in the village. The president was concerned that if there was unrest at the village, it could postpone the signing of the Ohrid Agreement, which was scheduled for Monday, 13 August 2001." Right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to unrest such as protests, no. Several of the soldiers who were killed on the 10th of August and who were killed by the Albanian terrorists at Ljubotenski Bacila locality, were from the village of Ljuboten. I believe that you can imagine what was the situation if several people are killed, several people from one village are killed, and why was the concern there. I didn't say that there were any unrest there is, but precisely what I explained here is what I meant. Ljuboten village and Ljubanci village are at a distance of two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Mr. Keskovski, there's nothing in what you've told us or in your statement that says that Johan Tarculovski was sent by the president to obtain information from the forces on the ground directly, is there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president had sent Mr. Tarculovski and ordered him to inform him from the ground itself. That is a broad order.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Keskovski, that Mr. Tarculovski was informed about the operation but that Mr. Tarculovski wasn't involved in the action at all. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what I stated in the statement, and I stand behind it. It is like that. The order of the president was specific: Go, since you will already be there, inform me about the situation on the ground where you are, the area of Ljubanci village.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Mr. Keskovski, I'd like you to turn to tab 7 of the Prosecution binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And for e-court purposes, I will be going to P303, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, this is a military report on the actions and situation of the area -- in the area of the 3rd Guard Brigade in the village of Ljuboten which was submitted on the 12th of August, 2001, which I believe you've seen before.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me, I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps it was the other report that was referred to. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just be shown the Macedonian version as well on the display?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: If I can just ask Madam Registrar to please move the page down so that the witness can see the first paragraph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, if I can just draw your attention to this first paragraph of this report, Mr. Keskovski, it says on the 10th of August, 2001, at 9.30 or 2330 hours a group of around 40 persons came to the school in the village of Ljubanci. The group was headed by the person Johan Tarculovski who comes and says - head of the agency Kometa - who comes from the village Ljubanci. After some time, more persons arrived whereby the number increased to around 60 to 70 persons. A Ministry of Interior truck arrived from which weapons, ammunition, bombs and bazooka were distributed to them. The persons were wearing Ministry of Interior uniforms. These persons asked Major Mitre Despodov, who is the commander of the 3rd Guardist Brigade to provide them with a place to sleep in the mountain lodge Ljubanci. And then it continues. It says that Major Despodov asked them on whose orders they had come and they said this is known to the president and no one else should know about their stay. Major Despodov asked them what their role is here and they answered that they had the task to enter into the village of Ljuboten and to conduct a cleaning of the terrain. So if Johan Tarculovski was not involved in this operation, Mr. Keskovski, how is it that he arrived there at 9.30 in the evening on the 10th of August with others from the Ministry of Interior and a truck full of weapons from the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I answer this question when this is not my Official Note and I can't answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't know that Johan Tarculovski was involved in the Ljuboten events. You are asking me now, you are presenting evidence to me, this is an Official Note of the army. I can't confirm anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: So when you say that you didn't know that Johan was involved in the action, you're basically -- you're just basing that on what -- and Johan told you basically, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you, please, to go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: If we can please have that displayed on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And if you can please look at the paragraph that starts with: "On Saturday, 11 August, 2001." Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO KESKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Now that says: "On Saturday, 11 August 2001, the above listed persons headed by Johan Tarculovski conducted a reconnaissance in the village of Ljuboten and in that village they shot at dogs and barked at them." And then it says: "Around 1700 to 1730 hours the person Johan Tarculovski asked Major Mitre Despodov to shoot at the target in the village of Ljuboten which they previously had determined precisely together with Major Mitre Despodov.
